t.4.66.1: Being praised thus, the mighty Hanumān began to grow in size; and, lashing his tail about, he attained great strength out of joy.
t.4.66.2: As he was being praised by all the foremost of the vānaras and was being filled with splendour, his form became unsurpassed.
t.4.66.3: Just as a full-grown lion stretches itself in a mountain cave, so now the true-born son of Māruta stretches and expands himself.
t.4.66.5: Rising from the midst of the monkeys, the hair of his body bristling with delight, Hanumān saluted the elder monkeys and spoke these words.
t.4.66.4: As the wise one yawned, his face shone forth, blazing like a heated frying-pan, like a fire without smoke.
t.4.66.7: I am the true-born son of that great-souled Māruta, swift in his rush and swift in his going; in leaping there is none equal to me.
t.4.66.6: Shattering the mountain peaks is Anila, the friend of fire: Vāyu, the wind, mighty and immeasurable, who ranges through the sky.
t.4.66.9: With the ocean driven forth by the force of my arms, I am able to flood the whole world together with its mountains, rivers and lakes.
t.4.66.8: For I could circle Mount Meru, vast and seeming to scrape the very sky, a thousand times over without hindrance.
t.4.66.11: I am able to circle a thousand times around Vainateya, the devourer of serpents, attended by birds, as he flies through the sky.
t.4.66.10: By the force of my thighs and shanks the ocean, the abode of Varuṇa, will surge up, its great crocodiles stunned senseless.
t.4.66.12: I am able to go up to the blazing, ray-garlanded sun, Āditya, setting out from his rising, and reach him even before he has set.
t.4.66.13: Then, O bulls among the leaping monkeys, without touching the ground, I can come back again with a mighty and terrible speed.
t.4.66.14: I would be able to surpass all who range through the sky; I shall churn up the ocean and I shall split open the earth.
t.4.66.16: Today the flowers of creepers, shrubs and trees on every side will follow me as I fly through the sky, and my path will be like the path of Svāti across the heavens.
t.4.66.15: O monkeys, as I leap I shall make the mountains tremble, and leaping over the great ocean I shall sweep it along with the force of my thighs.
t.4.66.17: O monkeys, all beings will see me as I rise up, as I move through the terrible sky, and as I descend again.
t.4.66.19: I shall scatter the clouds, I shall shake the mountains, and, leaping with a concentrated mind, I shall churn up the ocean.
t.4.66.18: O monkeys, you shall behold me, like the great Meru, going on my way covering the heavens, as though swallowing up the sky.
t.4.66.20: The power belongs to Vainateya, or to me, or to Māruta. Apart from the king of the Suparṇas and the mighty Māruta, I see no being who could follow me when I have leapt.
t.4.66.22: For as I leap across the ocean, my form will then be like that of Viṣṇu as he strode his three strides.
t.4.66.21: In the mere space of an eye's blink I shall suddenly plunge into the supportless sky, like lightning flashing forth from a cloud.
t.4.66.24: Equal to Māruta in force and equal to Garuḍa in swiftness, I shall go across ten thousand yojanas; such is my resolve.
t.4.66.23: With my understanding I clearly foresee it, and the impulse of my mind tells me the same: I shall see Vaidehī. Rejoice, O monkeys!
t.4.66.26: To him, the best of the vānaras, of boundless might, who was roaring thus, Jāmbavān, the most excellent of the monkeys, spoke, filled with great delight.
t.4.66.25: Striking boldly, I would snatch that amṛta from the hand of Vāsava, thunderbolt and all, or from the self-born Brahmā, and bring it here; or else I would heave up Laṅkā itself and go. Such is my resolve.
t.4.66.27: O hero, son of Kesarin, swift son of Māruta, the great grief of your kinsmen has been dispelled by you, dear one.
t.4.66.28: The foremost of the monkeys gathered here, who wish for your welfare, will with composed minds perform auspicious rites for the success of your mission.
t.4.66.29: By the grace of the sages, with the approval of the elder monkeys, and by the grace of your teachers, leap across the great ocean.
t.4.66.30: We shall stand on one foot until your return, and the lives of all the forest-dwellers depend upon you.
t.4.66.31: Then that tiger among monkeys spoke to those forest-dwellers: "This earth will not withstand my force when I leap."
t.4.66.32: For these peaks of this mountain Mahendra, crowded with dense masses of rock, are both firm and vast.
t.4.66.34: Then that monkey, the son of Māruta, equal to the wind and crusher of foes, ascended Mahendra, the best of mountains.
t.4.66.33: O best of leapers, these will bear the pounding of my feet as I leap a hundred yojanas from here.
t.4.66.35: The mountain was surrounded by trees of many kinds, its grassy meadows frequented by deer. It was crowded with creepers and blossoms, and its trees bore flowers and fruit in every season.
t.4.66.37: That mighty one, the best of monkeys, whose valour equalled that of Mahendra, roamed over Mahendra, the mountain lofty with its great peaks.
t.4.66.36: The mountain, roamed by lions and tigers and frequented by elephants in rut, resounded with the cries of flocks of impassioned birds and teemed with gushing torrents of water.
t.4.66.38: Pressed down by the feet of that great-souled one, the great mountain roared like a huge rutting elephant struck by a lion.
t.4.66.39: It let loose gushing torrents of water; its masses of rock were scattered, its deer and elephants terrified, and its great trees set trembling.
t.4.66.40: It was thronged with many pairs of Gandharvas, boisterous from their revels in drink, soaring up into the air, and with birds and hosts of Vidyādharas as well.
t.4.66.41: Then that great mountain became one whose great slopes were being deserted, whose mighty serpents had crept away into hiding, and whose peaks were shaken with rocks flung loose.
t.4.66.42: Then, with those hissing serpents half-emerged from their holes, the mountain appeared as if it were adorned with banners.
t.4.66.43: Being abandoned by the sages, who were bewildered with fear, the mountain sank down like a traveller deprived of his caravan, sinking in a vast wilderness.
t.4.66.44: That swift one, his whole being bent on speed, the foremost hero among the monkeys, slayer of enemy heroes, mighty and high-minded, composed his mind and went to Laṅkā in thought.
